https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world.text: At least three people were killed and over a dozen others injured after Russia launched an intense barrage of ballistic missiles and drones targeting Kyiv overnight into Saturday, local authorities said. A five-story residential building in the Solomianskyi District was damaged by falling debris with people believed to be still trapped inside and a fire in the courtyard, said Kyiv mayor Vitalii Klitschko in a post on Telegram. People were also reportedly trapped in another residential building the Shevchenkivskyi district, after a partial collapse on the first and second floors, Klitschko said. Elsewhere in the capital, warehouse buildings were on fire in the Darnytskyi district, he said. The attack came just two days after a large-scale Russian ballistic missile and drone attack across Ukraine killed 10 civilians and wounded more than 50 others and saw a Russian missile enter Polish airspace.

REUTERS/Gleb Garanich ( Reuters ) I vigili del fuoco intervengono sul luogo di un condominio colpito da un attacco con droni russi, nel contesto dell’offensiva russa contro l’Ucraina, a Kiev, Ucraina, l’11 settembre 2026. Per saperne di più By Olena Harmash KYIV, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Russia hit petrol stations in Kyiv on Tuesday and Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery, as the warring sides carried on with strikes on each other’s energy targets despite an announcement by U.S. President Donald Trump that they had agreed to stop. Russia launched 200 drones at Ukraine’s capital and other cities in overnight attacks, killing two people. In addition to petrol stations in Kyiv it struck energy and port infrastructure in other regions, Ukrainian officials said. For its part, Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery in Syzran in Russia’s Samara region on the Volga River, and also drone production facilities in the Taganrog and Oryol regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said. The Samara governor said an industrial facility was hit there without identifying it. The Taganrog governor said a warehouse of e-commerce firm Ozon was struck there. “Russia continues to attack our energy sector, regular logistics and critical infrastructure. And our responses to them for this are tangible,” Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app. Trump said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt strikes on each other’s energy infrastructure, which he says are the main factor in a global fuel shortage that has driven diesel prices in the United States to record highs. Zelenskiy said that Ukraine was ready to halt such strikes but required credible guarantees from its partners that Russia would also stop. Russia did not immediately comment on Trump’s announcement of an agreement but has previously welcomed calls from Trump on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries. Russia has been targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure with missiles and drones persistently since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and began targeting petrol stations in Kyiv and other cities in recent weeks. Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Russia this year, including a campaign targeting oil refineries that has caused fuel shortages. Previous attempts by the U.S. administration to broker a ceasefire on energy infrastructure have failed. EXPLOSIONS ROCK KYIV Ukrainian officials said that one person was killed in Russian attacks on Kyiv and another died in the city of Zaporizhzhia in the southeast of the country. Two petrol stations in Kyiv were damaged, the state energy company Naftogaz said. Reuters heard several explosions in Kyiv and the surrounding region. As Moscow’s attack on Ukraine was under way, neighbouring Poland held military aviation operations as a preventive step, Poland’s Armed Forces said, adding later that there was no violation of its airspace. In Lithuania, a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone early on Tuesday, the National Crisis Management Centre said. It did not say the origin of the drone. Similar incidents in the Baltic region in recent months have involved Ukrainian drones that Kyiv says were steered across NATO borders by Russian signal jamming. (Reporting by Olena Harmash in Kyiv, Anna Pruchnicka in Gdansk, Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo; Editing by Peter Graff) Di Olena Harmash Kiev, 15 settembre (Reuters) - Martedì la Russia ha colpito alcune stazioni di servizio a Kiev e l’Ucraina ha colpito una raffineria di petrolio russa, mentre le parti in conflitto hanno continuato a sferrare attacchi contro gli obiettivi energetici dell’avversario nonostante l’annuncio del presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump secondo cui avevano concordato di fermarsi. La Russia ha lanciato 200 droni contro la capitale ucraina e altre città in attacchi notturni, uccidendo due persone. Oltre alle stazioni di servizio a Kiev, ha colpito infrastrutture energetiche e portuali in altre regioni, secondo quanto riferito da funzionari ucraini. Da parte sua, l’Ucraina ha colpito una raffineria di petrolio russa a Syzran, nella regione russa di Samara sul fiume Volga, nonché impianti di produzione di droni nelle regioni di Taganrog e Oryol, ha dichiarato il presidente Volodymyr Zelenskiy. Il governatore di Samara ha affermato che in quella zona è stato colpito un impianto industriale, senza però identificarlo. Il governatore di Taganrog ha dichiarato che lì è stato colpito un magazzino dell’azienda di e-commerce Ozon. «La Russia continua ad attaccare il nostro settore energetico, la logistica ordinaria e le infrastrutture critiche. E le nostre risposte a questi attacchi sono tangibili», ha dichiarato Zelenskiy sull’app Telegram. Lunedì Trump ha affermato che l’Ucraina e la Russia avevano concordato di sospendere gli attacchi reciproci alle infrastrutture energetiche, che secondo lui sono il fattore principale della carenza globale di carburante che ha spinto i prezzi del gasolio negli Stati Uniti a livelli record. Zelenskiy ha affermato che l’Ucraina è pronta a sospendere tali attacchi, ma richiede garanzie credibili dai propri partner che anche la Russia si astenga dal colpire. La Russia non ha commentato immediatamente l’annuncio di Trump relativo a un accordo, ma in precedenza aveva accolto con favore gli appelli di Trump a Kiev affinché cessasse gli attacchi alle raffinerie russe. La Russia sta prendendo di mira con insistenza le infrastrutture energetiche ucraine con missili e droni da quando Mosca ha lanciato la sua invasione su vasta scala nel 2022, e nelle ultime settimane ha iniziato a colpire le stazioni di servizio a Kiev e in altre città. Quest’anno Kiev ha intensificato gli attacchi a lungo raggio contro la Russia, compresa una campagna mirata alle raffinerie di petrolio che ha causato carenze di carburante. I precedenti tentativi dell’amministrazione statunitense di mediare un cessate il fuoco sulle infrastrutture energetiche sono falliti. ESPLOSIONI SCOSSANO KIEV Funzionari ucraini hanno riferito che una persona è rimasta uccisa negli attacchi russi a Kiev e un’altra è morta nella città di Zaporizhzhia, nel sud-est del paese. Due stazioni di servizio a Kiev sono state danneggiate, secondo quanto riferito dalla società energetica statale Naftogaz. Reuters ha udito diverse esplosioni a Kiev e nella regione circostante. Mentre era in corso l’attacco di Mosca all’Ucraina, la vicina Polonia ha condotto operazioni di aviazione militare come misura preventiva, hanno dichiarato le Forze Armate polacche, aggiungendo in seguito che non vi è stata alcuna violazione del proprio spazio aereo. In Lituania, un caccia della NATO ha abbattuto un drone nelle prime ore di martedì, secondo quanto riferito dal Centro nazionale di gestione delle crisi. Non è stata specificata l’origine del drone. Incidenti simili verificatisi nella regione baltica negli ultimi mesi hanno coinvolto droni ucraini che, secondo Kiev, sarebbero stati guidati oltre i confini della NATO tramite interferenze di segnale russe. https://www.dw.com/en/eu-pulls-sponsorsh.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NzUl The conference took place at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius, but without several of its pre-planned backers [FILE: August 12, 2025] Image: Joko/picture alliance Advertisement The European Union on Thursday offered its reasons for withdrawing sponsorship for a disinformation event in Lithuania , following media reports claiming that it did so after pressure from the US government. The EU's foreign affairs division, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the governments of Canada and Lithuania all pulled their support from the event at short notice. Sponsors' logos on flyers and placards at the event were hastily covered over with paper strips. They withdrew participation in Disinfo2026 after pressure from the US State Department, according to reports in several media outlets, including the British newspaper The Guardian. What did the EU say about its decision? EU spokesperson Christian Wigand made no mention of the US or external pressure on Thursday but also did not repudiate the reports. "We were not comfortable with the framing of some of the discussions at the event," he told reporters in Brussels. "The organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU," he said. He refused to discuss details of which discussions or what framing had perturbed the EEAS. He also would not comment on whether there had been talks with US officials on the matter. "I'm not commenting on diplomatic exchanges as a matter of principle," he said. What signs of potential controversy at Disinfo2026 were visible? While a number of the sessions planned on the event's website across two days at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius appeared to have the potential to perturb more sensitive members of Donald Trump's administration, the opening two sessions on Wednesday morning stood out. The opening of the conference was an interview with Kimberly Prost, a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC) , which has come under sustained and heavy fire from Trump and his administration during his second term. This was followed by an hourlong session entitled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back," using the acronym for Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference. One of the planned speakers was a former CIA officer. Strong US free speech safeguards in the First Amendment to its Constitution mean the US has maintained a comparatively hands-off approach to combating disinformation — both in the political and legal spheres. This has arguably intensified, however, under President Donald Trump's leadership, with critics alleging it's partly because of his own often uneasy relationship with the truth.
